reviewer: Claude Code (AI assistant). Not an independent human review.
method: Single printed items split from the automatic families of 1801, and of 1800 where they reach the 1801 pages (long-running ones included), a sweep of word-for-word passages shared by 7 or more papers for short items the families miss, phrase searches on all 2,372 pages of 1801 in both transcriptions, reading of every hit, and scan checks of each admitted passage, by the one admission rule (9 or more papers admitted, 7 or 8 chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news)
scan_scope: Each crop covers the excerpt, the opening of the printed item. Long documents were not proofread in full.

new_groups.label: London, 17 August 1801: 'A second attack has been made upon the flotilla at Boulogne, and we are sorry to state, that it has not been attended with the desired success'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a London account of 17 August 1801 of the second attack by Lord Nelson's boats on the French flotilla at Boulogne: 'A second attack has been made upon the flotilla at Boulogne, and we are sorry to state, that it has not been attended with the desired success. Late last night the Providence cutter arrived at Dover with dispatches from Lord Nelson. The attack commenced at about a quarter flood, at 12 o'clock on Saturday night. Our squadron, consisting of 70 boats, was divided into four divisions'. The Alexandria Advertiser prints 'the desired effect' and 'on Sunday night', and the Portland Gazette 'very sorry'; the Republican Gazette leaves out the sentence on the Providence cutter; the Rhode-Island Republican prints the account from its third sentence, under the heading 'Second Attack on Boulogne'. All are counted together (C-02). A London paper's account at second hand of the dispatches.

new_groups.label: London, 15 August 1801: 'The intelligence of the surrender of Cairo is confirmed'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 15 August 1801: 'The intelligence of the surrender of Cairo is confirmed. Two messengers arrived yesterday with dispatches from Constantinople and Vienna to government and the East India Company. The dispatches to government are from Lord Minto, who continues to congratulate his majesty's ministers on the fall of Cairo. The dispatches, however, to the East India Company, place the intelligence beyond all doubt.' Five of the papers print after it the letter it introduces, from Peter Tooke at Constantinople of 19 July ('I had the honor to address you, on the 17th inst. by an express courier, in order to inform you of the reduction of the castle and city of Cairo by his majesty's and the Ottoman armies'), which is in 7 papers with the Rhode-Island Republican and the Republican Gazette and is not counted with it (see the README). new_groups.label: The sentence of the court martial on Captain George Little, 7 September 1801, with the Secretary of the Navy's letter of 25 September
new_groups.definition: Printings of the sentence of the court martial held on board the frigate Constitution on Captain George Little, of the frigate Boston, on charges brought by officers of the French corvette Le Berceau, which the Boston had taken in 1800: 'The Court, having heard all the evidence, and prisoner's defence, and maturely and seriously considered the whole, are unanimously of opinion, that the charges are malicious and ill-founded. The Court do, therefore, unanimously and honorably acquit the said Capt. Several papers print them after a Boston paper's comment on the trial ('The trial of Captain Little ... has excited much sensibility in the breasts of every real friend to the American navy'). new_groups.label: The preliminary articles of peace between Great Britain and the French Republic, signed at London on 1 October 1801
new_groups.definition: Printings of the preliminary articles of peace signed at London on 1 October 1801 by Lord Hawkesbury for the King and by Citizen Louis William Otto for the First Consul: 'His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great-Britain and Ireland, and the First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French people, being animated with an equal desire of putting a stop to the calamities of a destructive war, and to re-establish harmony and good understanding between the two nations'; the first article reads 'As soon as the Preliminaries shall be signed and ratified, sincere friendship shall be re-established'. dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1801 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 1,240 items printed somewhere; by the finder's count, with papers that have two catalogue numbers taken as one, 2 reach 9 papers, 8 reach 8 and 29 reach 7). The same script was run with year 1800 over the 1801 pages (items_from_1800.json: 154 items printed somewhere, none in more than 5 papers). Every item in 7 or more papers was read, and every item in 5 or 6 papers that a comparison of about 220 words of its text with every page put in more papers was checked. A sweep of the year for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 7 or more papers, as the 1803 review introduced (X-1803-09), found short items that the reuse families had not joined, and those were counted too. Every item that might reach 7 was counted again by its own words, in both transcriptions, and with phrase searches over all 2,372 pages of 1801, reading every hit.
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The one admission rule (R-01), as for 1776, 1800, 1802, 1803, 1804, 1805, 1806, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single printed item in 9 or more newspapers is admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; items are counted one by one; a sub-story may have fewer papers when its parent reaches 7. No year-specific threshold: items of 1801 reach 7, 8 and 9 papers. 6 to 10 papers are in print in any three weeks: 8 or 9 in January and February, 7 from March to June (8 in May), 6 in early July, 8 or 9 from mid-July and 9 or 10 from late September; from March to June an item in 7 papers was printed by every paper that survives for its weeks, and no item first printed in June reaches 7. Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01). Two items in 6 papers stand as sub-stories under parents that reach 7 (C-01), at the owner's decision of 23 November 2026: the merchants of New Haven's remonstrance, beside the President's reply to it, and the Knoxville paragraph that the treaty with the Cherokees is broken up, beside the Nashville paragraph on the treaty. Nothing is held back for its subject.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1801 has 14 catalogue series, which are 11 papers (C-04): the Portsmouth Oracle (sn83025544, The United States Oracle of the Day, to 10 October; sn83025545, the United States Oracle and Portsmouth Advertiser, from 17 October, by the same printers on the same day of the week); the Republican Ledger (sn84023378 to 17 November, number 13 of volume III; sn84023379, the Republican Ledger and Portsmouth Price Current, from 24 November, number 14); and the Wilmington Monitor (sn84020424, The Monitor & Wilmington Repository, total number 103 on 23 May; sn84038116, The Monitor, or Delaware Federalist, total numbers 120 and 146). The other eight papers have one catalogue number each: the Alexandria Advertiser and Commercial Intelligencer, the National Intelligencer, the New Hampshire Gazette, Jenks's Portland Gazette, the Providence Journal, the Virginia Argus (January and February only), Elijah Russell's Republican Gazette of Concord (24 issues) and the Rhode-Island Republican (from October). Every count takes each paper once.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item, one item of 1801 reaches 9 papers: the London account of 17 August of the second attack on the flotilla at Boulogne (9, with the Oracle's and the Portland Gazette's first sentences in other words and the Rhode-Island Republican's printing from the third sentence). Thirty-one items reach 7 or 8 papers: nineteen are chosen, ten are not, and two turn on private persons. Every other item is in 6 papers or fewer by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains items that papers printed together: General Augereau's note with the Frankfort report and other European news of January; the parts of the inaugural address with Mr. Jefferson's farewell to the Senate; the London news of August on Cairo, the attack on Boulogne and the rumour of peace; the Gibraltar news of November on Alexandria and the schooner Enterprize; the acts of the second session of the Sixth Congress through their enacting formula. Each text was counted by its own words. No act of that session reaches 7 papers by its own title followed by its enacting clause: the laws were printed in full by four papers at most (the National Intelligencer, the Oracle, Jenks's Portland Gazette and the Providence Journal); the act for the more convenient organization of the courts of the United States (the judiciary act of February 1801) is in 4.
counted_item_by_item.A sweep for short items: The reuse families join printings that share long passages, and the finder takes its candidates from them, so short items printed in many papers can be missed. As in the 1803 review (X-1803-09), every page of 1801 was swept for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 7 or more papers, and every passage found was counted by its own words. The sweep found two of the admitted items (the consul's circular of 15 May announcing the war with Tripoli; the Boston paragraph on Mr. Appleton's arrival with the ratified convention) and several items listed as not chosen (the Senate's confirmation of Mr. Dexter; the President and the kine pox; the telegraph to the Vineyard).
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item printed within different reports or in different translations counts as one (C-02): General Augereau's note within a Frankfort report in five papers and in other runs of news in two (7); General Moreau's report of Hohenlinden in three translations (2 + 4 + 1 = 7); Captain Baxter's journal under different introductions (7); Commodore Dale's letter in six papers and the same passage as a Boston paragraph in two (8); the London account of the attack on Boulogne with three first sentences (9); the preliminary articles of peace in the English text and in translations from the Moniteur and from French papers (8).
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: A paper that printed an item twice has two printings (C-08): the Oracle printed the preliminary articles of peace in its extraordinary of Wednesday 2 December and again in its regular issue of 5 December.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote, summarise or reci: Not counted (C-07): the inaugural address quoted in essays and comments (National Intelligencer, 6 March; Alexandria Advertiser, 9 March; Republican Gazette, 2 April and 28 May; Providence Journal, 17 June; Republican Ledger, 23 June; New Hampshire Gazette, 21 July; Portland Gazette, 26 October; Oracle, 31 October and 28 November) and printed in part as 'the governing principles of his administration' (Rhode-Island Republican, 17 October); the President's reply to the New Haven remonstrance quoted in essays and satire (Oracle, 1 August; Alexandria Advertiser, 3 August; National Intelligencer, 24 and 31 August; Monitor, 8 August; Portland Gazette, 16 November; Oracle, 12 December); the French First Consul's 'State of the Republic' summarised by five papers; the decree of St. Domingo on duties summarised by four papers; the chief of staff's report on the armistice of Steyer quoted in another account by two papers; the census returns given as a table by two papers.
counted_item_by_item.Letters and proceedings: The President's letter to Lieutenant Sterett and the lieutenant's answer are counted apart (8 and 7 papers): some papers print them together, others a week apart. The court martial's sentence on Captain Little and the Secretary of the Navy's letter approving it are printed together in all eight papers and are one item. The House committee's report of 19 February and Mr. Jefferson's answer are printed together in all seven papers and are one item. Paragraphs of the reports of the House's and the Senate's proceedings are counted by their own words (X-1800-08, X-1804-04); none of 1801 reaches 7.
counted_item_by_item.This year's printings: A reviewed year's group holds only that year's printings (C-11). The President's message of 8 December 1801, with his letter to the President of the Senate, is in 6 papers in 1801 (most papers printed it later in December or in 1802); General Augereau's note of November 1800 and General Moreau's report of December 1800 are admitted by their printings of 1801.
